newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says may use line-item veto on tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says may use line-item veto on tax bill.

text.p: President Clinton said Monday he may use his new line-item veto authority to strike some spending items from a $95 billion tax bill that he will sign with great fanfare Tuesday.
As the White House prepared a bill-signing ceremony for the South Lawn, Clinton went on a public relations offensive to convince Americans there is something for everyone in the legislation.
The bill aims to balance the budget by 2002 while at the same time cutting taxes by $95 billion, including a $500-per-child credit.
"It represents unprecedented opportunities and the means for all Americans to seize them," Clinton told the National Urban League.

But outside the White House's iron fence, dozens of protesters demonstrated against provisions in the bill that erodes the District of Columbia's home rule government powers in favour of a non-elected financial control board that will make key fiscal decisions.
"No freedom, no taxes!" they shouted toward the White House as police looked on.

In response, Clinton told a conference of the Urban League that, "I'm going to keep working until Washington D.C. is what the people of Washington and the people of the United States deserve for it to be."

During a picture-taking session in the Oval Office, Clinton told reporters White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles was leading an intensive review to see if there were any items in the bill that would be appropriate for the line-item veto.
Clinton said his experience as governor of Arkansas, where he had similar authority over state spending, showed "once I used it a few times I didn't need to use it very much anymore."
"I think if we have it, it ought to be used. I believe that it ought to be used somewhat sparingly," he said in a picture-taking session in the Oval Office.
After signing the bill Clinton will have five working days -- until next Monday -- to act.

The bill was passed by both houses of Congress last Thursday, the first tax bill to face the possibility of such a veto. The line-item authority allows the president to strip items from spending and tax measures without vetoing an entire bill.

Under the line-item veto law, Congress must identify for review tax breaks that apply only to a limited number of taxpayers. The congressional Joint Committee on Taxation has identified 79 such provisions.

One example is a tax break approved for New England producers of hard cider. Instead of being taxed at the same $1.07-a-gallon rate as wine, cider with an alcohol content below 7 percent would be taxed at 22.6 cents per gallon, less than half of what is charged for its major competition, beer.
Another example was the export credit that Microsoft and other computer software makers won for overseas sales.
Congress can override any line-item veto by a two-thirds majority in each house.
